modules.lesson:
### Separate the event into accountable tasks

This is study and training material, not operating or compliance instruction. The course pilot is non-credit. All facilities, operators, records, timestamps and readings in the examples are fictional. Numerical inputs are supplied case assumptions for teaching, not authorised operating values. Statutory reporting requirements are identified separately from those assumptions.

An adverse drinking-water event creates several responsibilities that can progress at different speeds. Internal escalation brings supervision and resources into the response. External reporting fulfils applicable legal duties. Protective and corrective action addresses the condition. Verification establishes whether the action worked. Closure records what has been completed, what evidence supports that conclusion and whether anything remains outstanding.

Do not let one task stand in for another. A supervisor's acknowledgement does not establish that the required external report occurred. An external incident reference does not prove that corrective action was implemented. A later acceptable result does not, by itself, establish that the original event is resolved.

Use a separate status for each task. Useful statuses include not started, attempted, acknowledged, underway, awaiting evidence and complete. Attach each status to an evidence reference and accountable person. “Reported and resolved” is too compressed to tell the next shift what happened or what remains exposed.

The practical question at handover is not simply whether someone responded. It is whether every required task has an identified owner, a defensible status and an explicit next decision. If an external contact is incomplete while a process correction is underway, both facts belong in the summary. Do not hide incomplete reporting behind successful treatment work, or dismiss completed protective work because other obligations remain open.

### Establish the reporting basis before interpreting progress

The Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 (Ontario), section 18, establishes adverse-result reporting duties. Use the Ontario adverse drinking water results technical bulletin to locate the applicable reporting requirements and exemptions, then check the current regulation governing the system and event. A bulletin supports interpretation; it does not replace the applicable legal text.

For Ontario adverse drinking water test results subject to reporting, an immediate verbal report is required, followed by written notice within 24 hours after that report. That written-notice period does not provide permission to defer the verbal report. Nor does contacting an internal supervisor replace applicable external reporting.

Establish who received the result, when they received it, what the result concerns and which duties apply to the parties involved. A laboratory's communication may be important evidence, but it must not be assumed to discharge every duty of an owner, operating authority or other obligated person. Confirm the applicable recipients, channels and responsibilities using the current requirements and facility reporting procedure.

Internal review should support accurate communication without becoming an unauthorised approval barrier. A result does not become reportable only when a manager agrees that it is serious. Conversely, do not invent a reporting category from a number alone. The result type, sampling context, system classification and applicable provisions matter.

O. Reg. 128/04 (Ontario), particularly sections 23 and 25–27, provides the relevant framework for operator designation, duties and records. Consult those provisions alongside the facility's designation records and procedures when assigning response roles. A shift roster identifies who is present; it does not necessarily establish who holds a particular designated responsibility.

If the result is disputed, separate the reporting question from the investigation question. Record the reason for the dispute and pursue clarification through the applicable process. An unsupported belief that a sample was contaminated is not evidence that the original record can be discarded. Retain the original result, the clarification request and any subsequent laboratory amendment as distinct records.

### Build a communication record that survives handover

A communication log should allow another operator to reconstruct what was known, what was communicated and what direction followed. Record the event identifier, communication time, recipient, channel, person reached, information supplied, acknowledgement, reference number and outstanding follow-up. Identify the time zone and distinguish the event time from the time the entry was created.

Use the following register structure during the training exercise. In real work, the facility's controlled form and reporting procedure govern.

| Record element | Evidence to enter | Judgment it supports |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger and receipt | Original result identifier, receipt time, recipient and sample identity | Establishes what initiated the response |
| Internal escalation | Person contacted, attempt time and acknowledgement time | Distinguishes notification attempts from confirmed awareness |
| External reporting | Required recipient, channel, person reached, time and report contents | Supports whether the applicable reporting pathway was completed |
| Directions | Issuer, exact direction, time, scope and confirmation of unclear wording | Establishes what follow-up was required |
| Action execution | Authorisation, executor, start and completion times, equipment or location | Connects a decision to an actual intervention |
| Verification | Method, location, instrument or laboratory record and acceptance basis | Tests whether the intervention achieved its intended result |
| Outstanding work | Named owner, dependency and next review point from the governing procedure | Prevents an unresolved task from disappearing at handover |

An unanswered call is an attempt. A voicemail is evidence of a message left, not necessarily evidence that an applicable reporting requirement was satisfied. A completed conversation should identify the person reached and what was conveyed. A call-duration record can corroborate contact, but cannot establish the conversation's contents by itself.

Where directions are unclear, obtain clarification through the applicable communication pathway. Preserve the original wording and the clarification rather than silently rewriting the first entry. If a direction is received verbally, record it promptly and identify who heard it. Do not paraphrase a conditional direction into an unconditional approval.

Late entries must remain recognisable as late entries. For example, a note entered after handover may describe an earlier call, but the record should show both times and its supporting basis. Preserve corrections through the controlled record process. Overwriting an incorrect timestamp destroys evidence about how the event was understood at the time.

### Worked example: calculate timing without declaring compliance

The fictional Cedar Inlet system receives a reportable adverse result. Supplied case assumptions are that the result was received on 12 May 2026 at 09:00, an internal supervisor acknowledged it at 09:01, and the required immediate verbal reporting communications were completed at 09:03. For this exercise, all required verbal recipients were reached at that recorded time. The written notice was submitted on 13 May at 08:40 through the required channel, with a retained submission confirmation.

The reporting requirement is not a supplied operating allowance. The Ontario requirement described above is immediate verbal reporting followed by written notice within 24 hours after that report. The exercise timestamps allow the learner to reconstruct the record and calculate the written-notice boundary.

First calculate the internal acknowledgement interval:

- Receipt time expressed after midnight: 9 h × 60 min/h + 0 min = 540 min.
- Internal acknowledgement time: 9 h × 60 min/h + 1 min = 541 min.
- Internal acknowledgement interval: 541 min − 540 min = 1 min.

Then calculate the interval to completed verbal reporting:

- Verbal reporting time: 9 h × 60 min/h + 3 min = 543 min.
- Elapsed interval from receipt: 543 min − 540 min = 3 min.

Next calculate the written-notice boundary and actual elapsed time:

- Written-notice boundary: 12 May 2026, 09:03 h + 24 h = 13 May 2026, 09:03 h.
- Time from verbal reporting to midnight: 24 h 00 min − 9 h 03 min = 14 h 57 min.
- Time from midnight to written submission: 8 h 40 min − 0 h 00 min = 8 h 40 min.
- Total elapsed time: 14 h 57 min + 8 h 40 min = 23 h 37 min.
- Margin before the boundary: 24 h 00 min − 23 h 37 min = 0 h 23 min.

Answer: the supplied written submission occurred 23 h 37 min after verbal reporting, which is 23 min before the calculated boundary. The supplied record therefore supports the timing element of the written notice, subject to confirming the correct recipients, content and submission evidence.

The 3 min interval does not establish a universal acceptable delay for immediate reporting. Review the actual sequence and circumstances rather than turning this example into a permitted waiting period. The internal acknowledgement also does not start the written-notice clock in this exercise.

If a draft notice existed at 08:40 but was not submitted, the calculation would establish draft preparation, not reporting completion. If different recipients were contacted at different times, retain those separate timestamps and confirm how the applicable requirements govern the written notices. Do not select whichever timestamp produces the most convenient result.

### Worked example: estimate the water volume requiring investigation

A separate fictional event at Cedar Inlet concerns an uncertain treatment-performance interval. This calculation supports investigation planning. It does not determine whether reporting is required, establish that unsafe water reached consumers or authorise a treatment response.

Supplied case assumptions are that the event review has identified an interval from 14:12 to 14:30, divided at a documented flow change at 14:20. The fictional validated flow record gives an interval-average rate of 36 L/s before the change and 24 L/s after it. For this example, the flow measurement point is the treatment outlet under investigation, timestamps are synchronised, and there is no unrecorded bypass across that measurement boundary.

Calculate each interval separately:

- First interval duration: 14 h 20 min − 14 h 12 min = 8 min.
- First interval in seconds: 8 min × 60 s/min = 480 s.
- First interval volume: 36 L/s × 480 s = 17,280 L.
- Second interval duration: 14 h 30 min − 14 h 20 min = 10 min.
- Second interval in seconds: 10 min × 60 s/min = 600 s.
- Second interval volume: 24 L/s × 600 s = 14,400 L.
- Total duration: 8 min + 10 min = 18 min.
- Total volume: 17,280 L + 14,400 L = 31,680 L.
- Metric volume conversion: 31,680 L × 1 m³/1,000 L = 31.68 m³.

Answer: under the supplied assumptions, 31.68 m³ passed the defined measurement point during the investigation interval. Retain the calculated value with its assumptions; it is not a claim of measurement precision beyond the supporting meter record.

A handwritten note instead uses the simple average of the two flow values. Check why that is unsuitable here:

- Simple average rate: (36 L/s + 24 L/s) ÷ 2 = 30 L/s.
- Total duration in seconds: 18 min × 60 s/min = 1,080 s.
- Unsupported estimate: 30 L/s × 1,080 s = 32,400 L.
- Difference from interval calculation: 32,400 L − 31,680 L = 720 L.
- Difference in cubic metres: 720 L × 1 m³/1,000 L = 0.72 m³.

The simple average gives equal weight to rates that persisted for unequal durations. Reject that method for these supplied records. If the rates were only isolated spot readings rather than defensible interval averages, neither calculation would establish the actual volume without further evidence.

The calculated volume is not automatically customer exposure. Storage, mixing, routing, isolation and travel time affect where water went. The investigation interval may also change if an instrument response delay or clock discrepancy is discovered. Retain the trend export, quality flags, meter identity, verification records, time-synchronisation evidence and valve-status records that support the measurement boundary.

US EPA's Generating high-quality turbidity data, EPA 815-B-19-010, is United States technical guidance, not Ontario law. Its measurement-chain and SCADA data-quality guidance supports checking instrument and data-system evidence before relying on a displayed trend. It does not establish Ontario reporting obligations or validate this fictional flow record.

### Define closure before the reassuring evidence arrives

Closure needs explicit criteria, not a general impression that the plant looks normal. Derive those criteria from applicable requirements, authority directions, the facility response procedure and event-specific verification needs. Identify what evidence will satisfy each criterion and who is accountable for reviewing it.

Keep reporting completion, operational verification and event closure distinct. Reporting may be complete while laboratory verification remains pending. An immediate process condition may be corrected while a required direction remains outstanding. A maintenance repair may be finished while the cause of the event is still uncertain.

For each corrective action, record the intended effect and the evidence needed to test it. “Instrument serviced” establishes maintenance activity. It does not establish valid readings unless the required verification evidence is also available. “Sample collected” establishes collection, not a laboratory outcome. “Authority contacted” establishes communication only to the extent supported by the contact record.

A later reading within a facility operating target describes a later condition. It does not reconstruct the earlier interval or prove that every required corrective step is complete. Compare evidence with predetermined criteria rather than selecting criteria that the available evidence happens to satisfy.

Where disinfection performance is involved, consult Ontario's Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water and the applicable facility approval and validated procedure. CT is condition specific. It depends on disinfectant, temperature, pH, residual and the approved hydraulic basis for that configuration. A recovered residual alone cannot establish adequate performance throughout an earlier event. Changed flow or configuration may invalidate the hydraulic basis used in an earlier assessment.

Assign every unresolved item to a named person or designated role, with a next review point drawn from the applicable direction or controlled process. Where permitted by the governing requirements, longer-term improvement work may remain separately tracked after immediate response tasks are completed. Do not use that separation to close mandatory corrective work prematurely.

A defensible closure summary states the original trigger, reporting evidence, actions, verification results, outstanding limitations and closure authority. It should also identify conditions that require reassessment, such as an amended laboratory report or newly discovered unreliable instrument data.

### Common errors

- **Calling the supervisor and marking external reporting complete.** Internal escalation and statutory reporting have different purposes and potentially different recipients. Retain separate evidence for each.
- **Treating a sent draft as a submitted notice.** File creation or an internal email does not prove delivery through the applicable reporting pathway. Check submission evidence and required recipients.
- **Using one acceptable reading to close the event.** The reading may support recovery at that location and time, but not earlier conditions or completion of required verification.
- **Replacing original records with corrected summaries.** This obscures what was known when decisions were made. Preserve originals, amendments and the reasons for changes.
- **Applying a sample result to the wrong location.** A clearwell sample cannot automatically establish conditions at every distribution location. Match sample identity and purpose to the closure question.

### What to verify before you act

For a real event, consult the current Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 (Ontario), section 18, the applicable drinking-water regulation and the Ontario adverse drinking water results technical bulletin. Confirm the reporting trigger, any applicable exemption, recipients, channels and required follow-up. Do not rely on an old exercise sheet or remembered deadline.

Consult the facility's applicable drinking-water approvals, including its Municipal Drinking Water Licence and Drinking Water Works Permit where applicable, together with the controlled adverse-result response procedure, reporting contact list, sampling plan and relevant validated treatment procedures. These establish the facility context that this training cannot supply.

Check designation and shift records against O. Reg. 128/04 (Ontario), sections 23 and 25–27, when confirming responsibilities. Review original laboratory reports, instrument records, communication logs, written-notice submission evidence and directions from the appropriate authorities. A summary cannot replace missing primary evidence.

Before recording closure, confirm who has authority to make that decision, which criteria apply and whether each criterion has supporting evidence. Before handover, state completed tasks, unresolved tasks, assigned owners and the next required review. Keep reporting, corrective action and closure separately visible until their own evidence supports completion.

modules.lesson:
### What a record has to carry besides the number

Every operational record has two halves. The content is the value, the observation or the statement. The provenance is everything that lets another person decide whether the content can be trusted: who observed it, who wrote it, when each of those happened, what instrument or document it came from, what units and time basis apply, and what was done to it afterwards. Auditors, medical officers of health, engineers doing a re-rating, and the operator on the next shift all rely on provenance more than on the number itself. A value with no provenance is an assertion. A value with provenance is evidence.

Ontario operator duties around records and entries sit in O. Reg. 128/04, sections 23 and 25 to 27, which deal with designation, duties and records, and adverse result reporting duties sit in section 18 of the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 together with the applicable adverse drinking water results technical bulletin. Those instruments tell you what must exist and who may make entries. They do not write your correction procedure for you. Your facility has an operational plan, a document and records control procedure and an Environmental Compliance Approval or drinking water works permit with its own record conditions. The training principle below is durable in any of them: preserve the original observation, make the change attributable, state the reason, and link the supporting evidence.

The measurement chain idea in the US EPA guidance on generating high quality turbidity data, EPA 815-B-19-010, is useful here even though it is US technical guidance and not Ontario law. It treats the sensor, the analyzer, the signal path, the SCADA tag, the historian compression settings and the report generator as one chain. A record is only as good as the weakest documented link in that chain. If you cannot say which tag a number came from, what its engineering units were, whether it was a one second sample or a fifteen minute average, and whether the historian applied deadband compression, then you cannot defend the number no matter how carefully you wrote it down.

### The four clocks and why they legitimately disagree

Operators get into trouble by assuming there is one time. There are at least four, and they routinely differ by minutes.

| Clock | What it means | Usual source of truth | Typical failure | What to record |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Event time | When the physical thing happened, for example when the filter effluent turbidity rose above the site action level | Historian at one second or short scan, corrected for known clock offset | Historian clock drift, deadband compression hiding the true onset | Raw timestamp, tag name, offset applied, scan or compression basis |
| Entry time | When a person wrote the record | The logbook entry or the electronic audit trail | Late entry presented as contemporaneous | Actual time of writing, plus the source used to reconstruct the event |
| Instrument time | The clock the device or historian stamped on the data | Device configuration record, last clock check | Never synchronised, daylight time handling, time zone set to UTC | Offset measured against the site reference clock, date of check |
| Receipt time | When information reached the person with the duty to act | Email headers, laboratory portal, phone log | Confusing lab report time with the time the operator became aware | Time received, time opened, who was notified and how |

An honest record can contain all four. "Event at 02:19 reference time, reconstructed from historian tag TU-201 with a measured offset of plus 5 minutes 30 seconds, entered 09:40 by operator A. Singh" is stronger than a clean looking single timestamp that quietly pretends the entry was made at the sink.

Receipt time matters most for adverse results. Under the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 and the applicable adverse result reporting provisions, an adverse drinking water test result requires an immediate verbal report to the specified parties, followed by a written notice within 24 hours after that verbal report. Never treat it as a several day allowance. Worked as arithmetic for a fictional case: the laboratory portal timestamp reads 16:42 on 8 May, the operator opens the notification at 21:10 on 8 May, the verbal report is made at 21:25 on 8 May. The written notice clock runs from the verbal report, so 21:25 on 8 May plus 24 hours gives 21:25 on 9 May as the outside limit for that example. All three times belong in the record, because a reviewer will ask why 16:42 and 21:10 differ and whether the notification path is adequate. Confirm the parties, the content and any exemptions against the current regulation and the technical bulletin, not against memory.

### Making an attributable correction

A correction is a new record about an old record. It never deletes the old one. On paper, draw a single line through the error so it stays legible, write the correction beside or below it, initial and date it, and add a short reason. Do not use correction fluid, do not overwrite, do not write over a digit to reshape it. In an electronic system, use the system's correction or annotation function so the audit trail captures both versions. If the system allows silent overwrite, that is a finding against the system, and you compensate by logging the change in a controlled correction register.

A defensible correction entry carries these fields.

| Field | Fictional example |
|---|---|
| Correction ID | COR-2025-041 |
| Original record ID and location | LOG-DW-08-14, daily distribution log, page 62, line 7 |
| Original content, preserved verbatim | "08:14 free chlorine 0.71 mg/L at D-17" |
| Corrected content | "08:14 free chlorine 0.71 mg/L at D-07" |
| What changed | Sample location identifier only. Value, units and event time unchanged. |
| Reason | Transcription error. Sample submission sheet SS-3318 and collector confirmation identify D-07. |
| Supporting evidence | SS-3318 scan, collector email 14 August 11:06, chain of custody CC-3318 |
| Author and role | R. Okafor, Operator in Charge |
| Correction date and time | 14 August, 11:12 |
| Downstream records affected | Weekly summary WS-33 reissued as WS-33 rev 1; laboratory report amendment requested |

Three judgment points. First, do not backdate. Writing the correction as though it was made at 08:14 destroys the audit trail and is worse than the original error. Second, do not edit someone else's original entry. You add your own attributable correction referencing theirs. Third, you cannot locally correct a laboratory report or any record issued by another party. You request an amended report and keep both the original and the amendment linked. If the amendment never arrives, the file shows an open discrepancy, which is an honest state.

When a field is genuinely unknown, preserve the uncertainty. A blank collection time that you fill in six hours later from memory becomes a false precision that a reviewer can often disprove from a gate log or a vehicle record. Write "collection time not recorded; collector states between 08:00 and 08:30 based on route sequence" and cite the source.

### Worked example 1: reconstructing a timeline across a historian clock offset

Supplied case assumptions for this teaching example only. Fictional plant, fictional readings. Site reference clock is the synchronised workstation clock. The historian is on a separate unsynchronised server.

Step 1. Measure the current offset.
Reference clock reading at check = 09:18:10
Historian clock reading at same instant = 09:12:40
Offset = 09:18:10 minus 09:12:40 = 0:05:30 = 330 s (historian is slow by 330 s)
Correction rule: reference time = historian time plus 330 s, at the date of this check.

Step 2. Convert the raw event window recorded on 14 March, the same day as the check.
Historian start of excursion = 02:14:00
Historian end of excursion = 02:41:30
Corrected start = 02:14:00 plus 0:05:30 = 02:19:30 reference time
Corrected end = 02:41:30 plus 0:05:30 = 02:47:00 reference time
Duration check = 02:47:00 minus 02:19:30 = 0:27:30 = 27 min 30 s

Step 3. Handle an earlier event, before the offset was known.
Previous documented clock check, 12 February, offset = 70 s slow
Current check, 14 March, offset = 330 s slow
Elapsed between checks = 30 d
Drift = 330 s minus 70 s = 260 s over 30 d
Drift rate = 260 s divided by 30 d = 8.67 s/d
Event of interest occurred 8 March, which is 24 d after 12 February
Interpolated offset = 70 s plus (24 d multiplied by 8.67 s/d) = 70 s plus 208 s = 278 s = 4 min 38 s
Raw historian start on 8 March = 02:14:00
Estimated reference start = 02:14:00 plus 0:04:38 = 02:18:38

Step 4. State the uncertainty honestly instead of the interpolated point alone.
Lower bound offset (no drift since 12 February) = 70 s, giving 02:15:10
Upper bound offset (full drift already present) = 330 s, giving 02:19:30
Reported result: estimated start 02:18:38 reference time, bounded 02:15:10 to 02:19:30, based on linear interpolation of a 260 s drift over 30 d.

Step 5. Confirm that duration is robust.
Drift within the event window = 8.67 s/d divided by 1440 min/d = 0.00602 s/min
0.00602 s/min multiplied by 27.5 min = 0.17 s
Answer: the excursion lasted 27 min 30 s, with drift inside the window contributing about 0.17 s, which is below the one second scan interval and therefore negligible. Start and end times in reference time on 14 March are 02:19:30 and 02:47:00. For the 8 March event, report 02:18:38 with the stated 02:15:10 to 02:19:30 bound.

The judgment: a constant offset changes when an event happened but not how long it lasted. Drift changes both, and it makes precision claims collapse if you never check the clock. If any CT or disinfection related claim depends on these timestamps, the Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water requires the contact time basis to match the approved hydraulic basis for that configuration, commonly expressed using T10, so a timeline reconstruction cannot be used to invent a contact time that the approval does not support.

### Worked example 2: reconciling logged daily volumes against the totalizer

Supplied case assumptions for this teaching example only. Fictional treated water meter, readings taken at 08:00 daily, all volumes in m3.

Step 1. Compute daily volumes from totalizer differences.
Day 1 to 2: 1 288 940 m3 minus 1 284 610 m3 = 4 330 m3
Day 2 to 3: 1 293 310 m3 minus 1 288 940 m3 = 4 370 m3
Day 3 to 4: 1 297 560 m3 minus 1 293 310 m3 = 4 250 m3
Day 4 to 5: 1 301 900 m3 minus 1 297 560 m3 = 4 340 m3
Day 5 to 6: 1 306 210 m3 minus 1 301 900 m3 = 4 310 m3
Day 6 to 7: 1 310 620 m3 minus 1 306 210 m3 = 4 410 m3
Day 7 to 8: 1 315 050 m3 minus 1 310 620 m3 = 4 430 m3

Step 2. Sum and cross check against the endpoints.
Sum of differences = 4 330 plus 4 370 plus 4 250 plus 4 340 plus 4 310 plus 4 410 plus 4 430 = 30 440 m3
Endpoint check = 1 315 050 m3 minus 1 284 610 m3 = 30 440 m3
The two agree, so the totalizer series is internally consistent.

Step 3. Compare with the handwritten logsheet.
Logsheet values = 4 330, 4 370, 4 520, 4 340, 4 310, 4 410, 4 430 m3
Logsheet sum = 30 440 m3 plus (4 520 m3 minus 4 250 m3) = 30 440 m3 plus 270 m3 = 30 710 m3
Discrepancy = 30 710 m3 minus 30 440 m3 = 270 m3
Relative discrepancy = 270 m3 divided by 30 440 m3 = 0.0089, which is 0.89 percent

Step 4. Effect on the reported average.
Logged seven day mean = 30 710 m3 divided by 7 d = 4 387.1 m3/d
Corrected seven day mean = 30 440 m3 divided by 7 d = 4 348.6 m3/d
Difference = 38.5 m3/d

Step 5. Decide, do not assume.
The pattern 4 250 written as 4 520 is a digit transposition, and the single day error is fully explained by it. But the totalizer only wins if it has supporting evidence: a current meter verification or calibration record, no logged meter fault, and no reset or rollover in the period. Answer: the corrected Day 3 volume is 4 250 m3 and the corrected seven day mean is 4 348.6 m3/d, conditional on meter verification record MV-2025-07 being current. If that verification is overdue, you record both series, flag the conflict, and escalate rather than quietly choosing the number you prefer.

Note what you must not do. Do not erase 4 520 and write 4 250. Do not adjust the other six days to make the total come out. Do not reissue the monthly summary without a revision number, because a summary that silently changes value between copies is the most damaging document in any audit.

### The evidence index and how summaries mislead

An evidence index turns a folder into a package a reviewer can follow. Give every source record a stable identifier and link each claim to the record that supports it.

| Record ID | Description | Source system or custodian | Period covered | Version | Location in package | Claim supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HIS-TU201-0314 | Turbidity tag export, one second scan, NTU | Historian, CSV export | 14 Mar 00:00 to 06:00 | rev 0 | Tab 3 | Excursion start and end times |
| CLK-0314 | Historian clock check sheet | Instrumentation technician | 14 Mar | rev 0 | Tab 3a | 330 s offset applied |
| LOG-DW-0314 | Shift log, page 62 | Paper logbook, scanned | 14 Mar | rev 0 | Tab 4 | Operator actions and entry times |
| COR-2025-041 | Correction entry | Correction register | 14 Aug | rev 0 | Tab 4a | Sample location changed D-17 to D-07 |
| LAB-3318A | Amended laboratory report | Licensed laboratory | 12 Aug sample | amendment 1 | Tab 5 | Corrected location on lab record |
| SUM-WS33 | Weekly summary | Supervisor | Week 33 | rev 1 | Tab 6 | Reported weekly values |

Misleading summaries usually are not lies. They are true statements that suppress the timeline. Common forms: a daily maximum that hides a two hour excursion because the reporting interval was a fifteen minute average; a statement that "all results were within limits" when one result was invalidated without documenting why; a rounded value carried into a summary while the raw record shows a value on the other side of the rounding boundary; a graph with the time axis cropped or the vertical scale truncated. For exported data, keep the units, the tag name, the parameter description, quality flags, the time basis and the export method with the file. A screenshot may illustrate a point, but if a retrievable export exists, the export is the evidence and the screenshot is an attachment.

### Common errors

First, backdating a late entry. An operator who writes at 09:40 an entry stamped 02:19 has created a false contemporaneous record. The defect is not the lateness. Late entries are normal and acceptable when identified as late. The defect is the false claim about entry time, which destroys the credibility of every other entry on the page.

Second, silently shifting timestamps to make records agree. If the historian is 330 s slow, you document the offset and show both raw and corrected times. Editing the raw export so it matches the logbook removes the only independent check you had, and a reviewer who finds the original export will treat the edited file as manipulated evidence.

Third, correcting a value when what changed was the identifier or the units. Changing D-17 to D-07 is a location correction. Changing 0.71 to 0.71 mg/L is a unit clarification. Neither should be recorded as if the measured value changed. Mixing these together in one vague entry such as "corrected result" makes it impossible to tell whether the instrument, the sample or the transcription was at fault.

Fourth, treating a screenshot or a personal notebook as the record of record. Personal notes are fine as a source for a reconstructed entry, but the controlled record must be the one the facility retains under its records procedure, and the note should be scanned and indexed if it supports a correction.

Fifth, resolving a conflict by discarding the record you distrust. Keep both, flag the conflict, state which one you relied on and why, and escalate if you cannot support the choice with verification evidence.

### What to verify before you act

Before you make or accept a correction, check these, in this order. Your facility Environmental Compliance Approval or drinking water works permit and any municipal drinking water licence conditions relating to records, sampling locations and reporting. Your operational plan and its document and records control procedure, which names who may make entries, how corrections are made and how long each record class is retained. The operator duty and record provisions in O. Reg. 128/04, sections 23 and 25 to 27, for who may make entries and what must be recorded. Section 18 of the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 together with the current adverse drinking water results technical bulletin for adverse result reporting duties, the parties to notify and any exemptions, remembering that the written notice follows the immediate verbal report within 24 hours. The Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water where the corrected record touches contact time, residual or the approved hydraulic basis, because CT is condition specific and depends on disinfectant, temperature, pH, residual and the approved basis for that configuration. The instrument calibration, verification and clock check records for any device whose data you are relying on. The laboratory chain of custody and the amendment process if the record originated outside your facility.

If you cannot name the document that authorises what you are about to write, stop and ask your Overall Responsible Operator. A delayed, correct, attributable record is recoverable. A fast, tidy, unsupported one is not.

### Fictional worked scenario: Maplebrook Water Treatment Plant

All facility names, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are supplied for this training example only. They are not authorized values and must not be applied to any real plant.

**Supplied records handed over at shift change**

1. Historian clock check sheet, 2 April: reference workstation clock read 14:06:05 at the instant the historian server clock read 14:03:20. No earlier clock check on file.
2. Historian export, tag TU-303, Filter 3 effluent turbidity, one second scan, NTU. Values remain above the site action level stated in the plant operational plan continuously from 03:48:00 to 04:05:00 historian time on 2 April.
3. Handwritten shift log entry, written at 07:10 on 2 April: "Filter 3 turbidity bump around 03:45, lasted about 10 minutes, cleared on its own." No source cited.
4. A printed screenshot with no time axis, no tag name and no date, annotated by hand "peak 0.62 NTU".
5. Daily summary signed at 08:00 on 2 April: "No turbidity excursions this shift."

**What to reject and why**

Reject record 5 outright. It contradicts a one second historian export from the same period and no invalidation record exists. Reject record 4 as standalone evidence. Without a tag name, date or time axis it cannot be tied to the event, and a retrievable export exists, so the export is the evidence. Record 3 is retained but its two numeric claims are not relied on: the 03:45 start has no stated source, and the 10 minute duration conflicts with the export.

**Worked reconstruction**

Offset = 14:06:05 minus 14:03:20 = 0:02:45 = 165 s, historian slow.
Corrected start = 03:48:00 plus 0:02:45 = 03:50:45 reference time.
Corrected end = 04:05:00 plus 0:02:45 = 04:07:45 reference time.
Duration = 04:07:45 minus 03:50:45 = 0:17:00 = 17 min 0 s.
Logged duration = 10 min. Understatement = 17 min minus 10 min = 7 min.
Relative understatement = 7 min divided by 17 min = 0.41, which is 41 percent.

Only one clock check exists, so drift cannot be interpolated. Record the offset as measured on 2 April and flag that no bounding is possible until a second check is performed.

**Actions**

Raise correction entry COR-2025-058 against the daily summary, preserve the original wording, state the reason and cite the export and the clock check sheet. Index the records as HIS-TU303-0402, CLK-0402, LOG-0402 and SUM-0402 rev 1. Keep record 3 in the package as an unsupported contemporaneous note. Confirm against the plant operational plan and the Environmental Compliance Approval whether this excursion triggers any notification duty before closing the file.

checks.prompt: A logbook line reads only "turbidity 0.18". Using the module's content and provenance idea, what is the main weakness of this record?
choices: It carries content but no provenance, so another person cannot judge whether the value is trustworthy
It carries provenance but no content, so the reviewer cannot tell what value was actually observed
It is acceptable because the shift supervisor can recall the instrument and the sample point later
It is acceptable because the historian will always hold a matching tag value for that same minute
checks.explanation: Provenance is who observed, who wrote, when each happened, the instrument or tag, the units and the time basis. Without it the number is an assertion rather than evidence. Relying on later recall is exactly the false precision the module warns against, since memory cannot be verified by a reviewer.

checks.prompt: A paper daily log entry shows the wrong sample location. Which method best preserves the original observation while making the change attributable?
choices: Cover the wrong text with correction fluid and print the right location neatly above it
Draw one line through the error, write the correction, then initial, date and give a reason
Reshape the written characters so the entry reads correctly without any added markings
Erase the line and rewrite the whole entry so the page stays clean for the auditor
checks.explanation: A single legible strike through plus correction, initials, date and reason keeps both versions visible and attributable. Correction fluid, overwriting or erasing destroys the original observation, which is the very thing an auditor needs to compare against.

checks.prompt: Which description matches receipt time as defined in this module?
choices: The moment the physical condition occurred in the process, as held by the historian
The clock value the analyzer or historian server stamped onto the stored data point
The moment information reached the person who carries the duty to act on it
The moment a person actually sat down and wrote the entry into the logbook
checks.explanation: Receipt time is when information reached the person with the duty to act, evidenced by email headers, portal records or phone logs. The other options describe event time, instrument time and entry time, which legitimately differ from receipt time and are often confused with it.

checks.prompt: Fictional site. A clock check shows the historian is slow by 240 seconds against the site reference clock. A raw historian timestamp for an alarm reads 03:12:00 on the same day. What is the reference time?
checks.explanation: If the historian is slow, reference time equals historian time plus the offset, so 03:12:00 plus 4 minutes is 03:16:00. Subtracting to get 03:08:00 is the common error of applying the offset in the wrong direction, which would place the event earlier than it truly happened.

checks.prompt: An accredited laboratory report lists the wrong sample location for a distribution sample. What is the defensible operator action?
choices: Request an amended report and keep the original and the amendment linked in the file
File the report unchanged and note nothing, since the laboratory owns that document
Retype the report with the right location and store only the retyped corrected version
Strike the location on the report, write the right one, then initial and date the change
checks.explanation: A record issued by another party cannot be locally corrected. You request an amendment and keep both versions linked, and if it never arrives the file honestly shows an open discrepancy. Marking up the laboratory report yourself creates a document that neither party can defend.

checks.prompt: A sample collection time was left blank and is noticed six hours later. Which entry best preserves the uncertainty?
choices: Leave the field blank permanently and add no explanation of why it was never filled
Record that time was not noted, state the collector's stated range and cite the source
Enter the scheduled route time, since that is the time the collector normally arrives
Enter 08:15 because the collector believes that is roughly when the sample was taken
checks.explanation: Stating that the time was not recorded, giving the bounded range and citing the basis keeps the record honest and checkable. Writing a single confident time from memory creates false precision that a gate log or vehicle record can often disprove, which damages the credibility of the whole file.
